subject: brutalistBlock
pitch:
Category: Architecture.
Subject: brutalist housing block.
Style: raw concrete brutalism.
reasoning:
I'm planning a static brutalist housing block model using the SDK, skipping joints since nothing needs to move, and sketching out realistic dimensions—a slab roughly 48m wide, 18m deep, and eight storeys tall.

I'm adding a taller stair/lift tower, piloti ground-floor columns, egg-crate balcony frames with recessed dark windows, and a parapet with cantilevered water tank boxes. For the concrete, I'm planning mottled paint with subtle streaking and board-marked formwork lines, keeping texel density coarse given the large surface area, and reserving finer paint detail for weathering stains beneath balconies rather than everywhere.

Rethinking the egg-crate facade, I realize per-bay boxes would balloon into hundreds of parts, so I'm switching to long continuous boxes per floor for slabs and parapets, plus full-height vertical fin walls at bay divisions, which gives the same brutalist look with far fewer parts. For windows, I'm planning a single tiled texture per floor band covering all twelve bays, reused across floors and both sides to avoid redundant geometry.

I'm also sketching out the texture content: a dark recessed concrete background with randomized glass panel colors (orange/blue, some lit) generated deterministically via code, sized to roughly two-thirds of the floor height. Then I'm laying out the overall massing -- piloti height, floor stack height, main wall block dimensions, and balcony depth -- before placing chunky square piloti columns at regular intervals.

Now I'm adding paired columns along the front and back facades, plus a glazed ground-floor lobby box centered between them. I'm also planning two projecting stair/lift towers at opposite ends with slit-window textures, connected by occasional bridging slabs between floors.

For the roof, I'll add a plant room box on top with an offset, paired water tank cylinders, and vertical louvres to break up the massing, keeping the rooftop elements simple rather than adding a cantilevered penthouse.

For the concrete texture, I'm deciding against stretched board-mark textures on each box face and instead opting for a paint-based approach with faint horizontal lines spaced roughly every 0.2m to simulate formwork boards at a workable texel density.

Rather than pour-line textures or tie-hole dot grids, which turn out too faint at reasonable resolution, I'm calculating the total surface area needed and settling on noise-based staining combined with a base concrete tone that varies spatially to give a convincing weathered look without discrete texture mapping issues.

Now I'm defining paint functions for the stains—vertical streaks under ledges using stretched noise, top surfaces lightened where sun-facing, and moss/dirt darkening near the base. I'm also setting up the color palette: concrete tones for the main structure and shadowed fins, roof color, and flat colors for glass, dark trim, and rust accents, before moving into building the windows/facade texture generator.

Writing facade SVG texture...

I'm computing the slab positions per floor and parapet placement, then thinking about selective glow for lobby glass and rooftop warning lights rather than lighting every window. Next I'm sketching the backside gallery with its walkway deck and parapet wall.

For the back wall I'm planning a different window/door texture pattern, alternating bays, and being careful about plane orientation and facing direction so the texture reads correctly from outside. I'm also considering adding a tall vertical slit window or mural on the blank end gable walls.

I also want some painted signage on the end wall, like "ALDER HOUSE" lettering, plus a colorful concentric-arc mural on the gable. For the piloti columns, I'm using tapered frustum boxes that are wider at the top than the bottom for visual interest.

Then I'm adding a glass-box lobby between the pilotis, a cantilevered entrance canopy supported by thin rods, entry steps, and a triangular-profile accessibility ramp extruded along the side.

I'm skipping an unnamed ground plinth, giving the roof a parapet made of boxes, and capping each tower with an overhanging slab that holds slit windows. For those slit windows I'm making a transparent texture plane where only narrow vertical slits glow, so the tower facade reads as glowing lines against a dark surface.

Working out the exact tower dimensions and slit placement now — sizing each tower, positioning the slit planes on the front and side faces, and figuring out how many floors' worth of slits to draw in the SVG, maybe using a stair-step zigzag pattern for visual interest. Writing SVG slit texture...

I'm also sketching the roof elements: rooftop water tanks as octagonal cylinders on legs, boxy chimneys with cap slabs, and an antenna with a glowing red light, plus plant rooms and parapets sized against the roof slab height. I'm considering adding brise-soleil fins and a recessed vertical slit at the gable end, but deciding the colored infill panels already provide enough visual accent so I can skip extra painted soffits.

Scattering small random details now -- occasional crates or plants on balcony slabs grouped by color for merging, plus tilted satellite dish geometries collected separately, all built from indexed three.js primitives compatible with mergeGeometries. I'm then planning the vertical fin spacing along each facade at regular bay intervals.

Working out slab, parapet, and fin dimensions per floor, reducing fin frequency on the back facade while keeping the front fully detailed, and considering adding occasional colored panel inserts into the parapet for visual variation every few bays.

Writing concrete paint function...

Adding pour-line streaking...

I'm also adding grime darkening near ground level and extra brightness on upward-facing surfaces catching top light, then considering a cheap darker concrete variant for recessed or dirty roof elements.

I'm sketching helper functions: a part-adding method that places box geometry at a given point, a floor baseline at y=0 so pilotis and lobby elements sit flush, and a textured plane helper for signage that takes position, direction, axis, and texture inputs.

Now I'm working through facade dimensions—placing window planes slightly offset from the main wall box so they don't z-fight, aligning fin boundaries with window bay spacing across twelve bays, and sizing the main body box and roof slab with their vertical center offsets.

Defining floor slabs by level, with the top of each slab computed from the base height plus floor spacing, and pilotis columns set at regular x-intervals with their tops around y=4.2. I'm also placing the glass lobby box centered near the ground floor entrance.

Removing the piloti that would collide with the entrance opening and designing the glowing lobby glass front with a warm interior gradient, dark mullions, a door, and faint figure silhouettes. I'm also considering placement for the "ALDER HOUSE" sign near the entrance canopy.

Actually I should put a mural there instead. I'm reconsidering the gable placement since the end tower overlaps too much of that wall — I'll reposition Tower A further back along the z-axis so there's clear gable space for the mural and lettering.

Tower A spans roughly x 24 to 29.5, z centered at 0 with depth 7, rising from ground to y 34 with a solid lower portion and piloti gap above, capped with a stacked slab and small lift-machinery box. I'm treating it as attached to the gable face rather than bridged separately. Now I'm positioning tower B, centering it around x=-9.

Tower B sits around z=-8, 5 wide and 5 deep, standing 32 tall, with slit window planes on its facing sides and back gallery slabs partially tucked inside the tower volume where they won't be visible. I'm now designing a reusable slit-texture generator that produces a zigzag stair pattern scaled to each tower's floor count and height.

Writing slit texture SVG...

For tower A's +z face I'm sizing the slit plane to span its nine floors from 4.5 to 32.4 meters, and for tower B covering eight floors from 4.5 to 29.3, both matching their respective tower heights. I'm also working out the back facade texture with alternating door and kitchen window bays, keeping in mind the gallery parapet at 1.1m will hide the lower portion of each door for a realistic look, and deciding whether to use a solid concrete-colored background or transparency to reveal the underlying wall material.

Switching to transparent backgrounds for both front and back textures so openings read correctly against the painted wall beneath, then designing the front bay layout: a dark recessed frame, a sliding glass door panel with highlight and mullion details plus a random curtain overlay, and an infill panel containing a smaller slit window, with some bays getting warm lit-window treatment instead of glass. I'm also confirming the SDK's rng function returns a callable random generator for these randomized touches, and starting to plan the equivalent back-facade texture logic.

Alternating back-wall bay layouts between a door-plus-kitchen-window pairing and a wide two-pane window, then adding balcony clutter like pots, bikes, and chairs as merged boxes, scattering satellite dishes along the front parapet, and considering AC units on the back wall before deciding to skip them along with window sills and rooftop railings. I'm also noting the rooftop already has plant rooms, tanks, chimneys, and lights, and settling on using a darker, warmer concrete tone for the fins versus the standard tone for the slabs.

Now I'm tallying up the total part count toward a 180-340 target, adding back-gallery ribs, rainwater pipes, entrance steps, planters, bollards, and a ramp to round things out, and planning the texture set including separate slit textures for the two different floor counts plus a freestanding sign slab near the entrance reading "ALDER HOUSE."

Setting up the builder with proper typing...

Still writing concrete shader...

Merging each group's geometry into a single mesh placed at the origin since there are no joints to attach to, then setting up the main building dimensions: eight floors at 3.1 units each, a ground height of 4.5, giving a total height of 29.3, with the building footprint at 48 by 11.

Still defining wall and slab geometry...

Checking the roof slab coverage over the fins - roof spans y 29.15-29.65 near wall top at 29.3, with overhang depth covering z ±6.3 while fins reach to 7.1, so I need to confirm fin tops align properly under the roof overhang.

I'm sizing the roof slab to depth 14.6 (z -7.3 to 7.3) with position centered at TOP+0.1, then adjusting fin heights to run from G-0.35 up to TOP so they tie cleanly into the underside of the slab. For the parapet I'm placing four boxes along the roof edges (front/back at z=±7.0, ends at x=±24.2) at height TOP+0.375, each 0.9 tall, then setting the plant top elevation and starting to lay out front window planes along the facade.

Now I'm working out the back facade: window bottom/top heights to match the front, a back gallery slab spanning z -5.5 to -7.3, and a parapet strip at z=-7.2. I'm noting the rotated plane orientation for back-facing windows (dir [0,0,-1]) and planning dark downpipe cylinders at four x-positions along the rear, plus rear piloti columns around z=-4.2. I'm now starting to block out Tower A as a large concrete box.

Generating tower geometry...

Adding a dark stroke outline for definition, checking it stays thick enough at the target resolution to render clearly.

Now I'm blocking out the lobby structure: the main box, glass entrance plane, canopy with support pillars, and front steps, all sized and positioned to sit flush with the floor. I'm also considering front planters to break up the base facade.

Still placing site details...

Now I'm adding rooftop structures: a plant room box with its own roof slab, plus a row of dark louvre bars across its front face for detailing.

Then I'm designing two cylindrical water tanks on stands, with cone-shaped domed lids and simple ladder details, painted in a muted metal gray tone before moving on to chimney shapes.

Now for the chimneys: a trio of narrow boxes with capped tops placed near the building's edge, plus an antenna rod with cross bars and a glowing red light sphere on the tower, and I'm planning out the pilotis support columns along the base.

For the pilotis, I'm placing tapered frustum columns at regular x-intervals along both front and back edges, using a box-taper shape to get that chunky brutalist look rather than round cylinders, with flat bottoms resting on the ground. I'm also adding end shear walls beneath the structure for added support.

For the mural plane on the west facade, I'm defining a tall panel with a design featuring a large rust-colored sunset circle with concentric ochre and cream rings, diagonal bands, and bold vertical "ALDER HOUSE" lettering in cream against the wall.

Now I'm setting up random balcony prop placement per floor and bay, rolling for occasional items like plant pots.

Then I'm adding scattered satellite dishes mounted at parapet height using partial dome-shaped sphere geometry.

Solving for the rotation angle, I get roughly -2.214 radians to orient the dome correctly, but I need to check whether the concave side will actually be visible from the front or if it'll render as a backface instead.

Switching approach, I'll use a shallow cylinder as a disc instead of dealing with the concave sphere issue, rotating it to face front-upward with a calculated axis angle, plus a thin box for the arm piece. Now I'm picking out a color palette for the panels.

Writing facade texture code...

Setting the finishing color to the darker concrete tone, and defining tone values for the concrete palette variants. Now I'm writing the generation code with nested loops building up the palette array and flushing the final output.

Adding window glass, downpipes, and parapet post geometry...
